content:
Based on a Times of India report from Dehradun. We update this post when organisers confirm new details.

Corbett Tiger Reserve is known for its tigers, its river valleys and its sal forests. It now has another claim on visitors' attention. Its first literature festival, titled 3 Days in the Wild, began in Ramnagar. It brings writers, conservationists, historians, storytellers and photographers into one of India's best-known wildlife landscapes.

If you are planning a trip to Uttarakhand, or you are considering a second home near Jim Corbett, events like this are one more reason to spend time in the region. Here is what the festival is for and why it matters.

Reports describe a four-day event at Corbett Tiger Reserve, with sessions centred on nature, wildlife, the Himalayas and the heritage of Uttarakhand. Nearly 30 participants are taking part, and the programme runs across three venues. This is the first time a festival of this kind is being held inside the reserve.

Corbett director Saket Badola said the festival is being organised with support from the Uttarakhand forest department, Corbett Tiger Reserve and Uttarakhand Tourism.

A note on the name: the festival is titled "3 Days in the Wild", while reports mention four days. If you plan to attend, confirm the exact dates and session timings with the organisers before you travel.

The line-up mixes literature, history, field naturalism and photography:

  • Namita Gokhale, Sahitya Akademi Award-winning author and co-founder of the Jaipur Literature Festival.
  • Shekhar Pathak, historian known for chronicling the Chipko movement.
  • Stephen Alter, author and naturalist.
  • Anup Sah, Padma Shri awardee, photographer, mountaineer and environmentalist.

The combination reflects how the region is understood. Hill communities, forests, climbing, photography and history are closely linked in Uttarakhand, and the programme treats them together.

Conservation and local people. Forest minister Subodh Uniyal said conserving forests and wildlife has to go together with improving the lives of local people. Reserves sit alongside villages whose livelihoods depend on the same region, so this balance is a recurring concern in conservation.

Corbett's wider identity. Principal secretary R K Sudhanshu said the world associates India with the Himalayas and with Corbett, and that the festival could widen that identity.

Community involvement. Chief wildlife warden Neena Grewal said the event brings together the forest department, entrepreneurs linked with it and the local community. She expressed hope that it would become an example for others.

A literature festival inside a tiger reserve is an unusual format, and it points to a few things:

  • A broader reason to visit. Corbett has mostly drawn people for safaris. Cultural programming gives travellers another reason to come, and may encourage stays outside peak wildlife-viewing windows.
  • Local participation. The stated involvement of the community and forest-linked entrepreneurs suggests an effort to spread the benefits locally.
  • Responsible tourism. Pairing talks with guided walks encourages visitors to learn about the ecosystem rather than only look for sightings.

Whether the festival becomes an annual fixture is not yet known, and no official announcement on that appears in the reports.

title: Beyond Flats and Farmhouses: The Rise of Resort-Style Plotted Townships in India

content:
A resort-style plotted township is a planned residential community where buyers purchase individual plots within a boundary-walled layout that also includes shared amenities such as a clubhouse, landscaped common areas and managed internal roads. It sits between two formats Indian buyers already know well: the urban flat, where you own a unit inside someone else's building, and the standalone farmhouse, where you buy land and manage everything on it yourself. This format combines the parts of each that buyers tend to value most: direct land ownership, and a managed, amenity-rich setting that doesn't ask the owner to build every piece of infrastructure alone.

To make this concrete, this piece looks at how the category works in practice through The Koru Ville, a RERA-approved resort-themed plotted development by Sumiram Sai Realtors near Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand, based on details published on the project's own page. What's on offer there is land — resort-themed plots within a planned, amenity-equipped community — with an associated design plan for owners who choose to build a private villa in Uttarakhand.

What a Resort-Style Plotted Township Actually Is

The phrase gets used loosely, so it helps to be specific about what typically distinguishes this format from other rural or semi-rural property types.

A plotted township is, first, a planned layout. Instead of buying an undivided piece of agricultural or rural land and arranging access and utilities independently, buyers get a demarcated plot within a layout that already has internal roads, defined plot boundaries and, in stronger projects, utility connections either in place or on a stated rollout.

Second, it's gated. A boundary wall and controlled entry are close to standard for this category, offering a level of security and privacy that a standalone rural plot typically doesn't.

Third, it's amenity-led. This is the "resort-style" part. Common facilities — a clubhouse, walking or jogging trails, landscaped gardens, sometimes a shared pool or play area — are built and maintained at the community level, giving every owner access to more than they'd typically build for themselves on a single plot.

Fourth, the core product is the plot. What varies between projects is what comes attached to it — in some cases just the boundaries and community infrastructure, in others a design plan owners can follow when they're ready to build, so that the community develops a consistent, cohesive character over time.

Why This Format Has Been Gaining Attention

A few genuine shifts in buyer behaviour help explain why this category has grown, particularly around weekend-home markets near major Indian cities — the Lonavala-Alibaug belt near Mumbai, parts of Coorg and Chikmagalur near Bengaluru, and hill and Terai corridors near Delhi-NCR are commonly cited examples in real estate commentary.

Hybrid and remote work has changed what a second home needs to do. A property once meant purely for occasional holidays now sometimes doubles as an occasional workspace, which raises expectations around comfort and reliability.

Buyers increasingly want land ownership without the full weight of land management. A farmhouse offers a large plot and full control, but also full responsibility for security, water, road access and upkeep, often from a distance. A managed plotted community shifts much of that operational load to a community structure.

Interest in an investment in resort-style property has grown alongside interest in more conventional real estate. For some buyers, land within a managed, amenity-led community feels like a more tangible middle ground than a financial instrument, while still requiring the same care around documentation and realistic expectations as any property purchase.

These are observed shifts in what buyers say they want, offered as general analysis rather than a projection of future prices or resale demand for any specific market.

Typical location Urban/suburban Rural, often distant from services Semi-rural, often near tourism or nature destinations

Each format suits a different priority. A flat suits buyers who want convenience and don't mind shared decision-making. Both approaches have their own strengths. An open design gives buyers more freedom over construction cost, timeline and style. content:
Imagine standing in an open forest clearing as morning light spills through tall grass. A herd of elephants moves slowly past you. Somewhere deeper in the trees, a tiger walks without a sound. That picture lives in the heart of every traveller who dreams of a Jim Corbett safari. Yet most people believe a safari means picking a date and showing up at a gate. The truth feels far more interesting. This park splits into many tourism zones, and each zone gives you a separate world.

Some zones stand out with tall grass and elephants, while others hide dense sal trees where tigers roam. A few stay open all year, while others close when rain arrives. Because of this, Jim Corbett safari zones deserve a closer look before you book anything. Picking the wrong zone can leave you disappointed. Picking the right one turns a simple trip into a story you tell for years. This blog guide walks you through every major zone, starting with Phato, so your first safari feels magical.

Why Corbett Is Divided Into Different Zones

Jim Corbett is not one big open playground. Forest officers divide Jim Corbett safari zones for good reasons. Wildlife needs protection, and visitors need management. Permits stay limited, so animals do not feel crowded. Each zone carries its own gate, its own rules, and its own season. Some zones open in winter, while others welcome guests during monsoon. This system keeps the forest healthy and the experience special. Understanding this system helps you plan a smarter Jim Corbett itinerary and avoid common mistakes.

Phato Zone – Corbett's Fast-Rising Wildlife Destination

Phato Zone is located near the Kashipur–Ramnagar corridor. This zone has gained attention because it offers a calm, less crowded safari zone. Phato Gate serves as the entry point, and it is close to several resorts and townships; it opens 365 days a year for visitors, even in the monsoon. Many travellers now choose Phato because it blends easy access with real forest beauty.

What Makes Phato Special

  • Phato Gate opens doors to rich buffer forest land.
  • The terrain mixes open patches with thick trees.
  • Deer, wild boar, and elephants often appear here.
  • Birdlife flourishes, so photographers stay busy.
  • Crowds stay smaller compared to famous zones.
  • The drive from Ramnagar feels short and smooth.

Phato works well for families and first-timers. Children spot animals without waiting for hours. Couples enjoy quiet moments under tall trees. Because Phato Gate exists near growing residential areas, many visitors combine a safari with a longer stay. This zone also pairs nicely with a Jim Corbett weekend trip, since you can reach it fast and still enjoy deep forest vibes.

Pros of Phato Zone

  • Fewer vehicles mean a peaceful ride.
  • More chances to see elephants and deer.
  • Easy access from nearby townships.
  • Perfect for short trips and quick getaways.

Cons of Phato Zone

  • Tiger sightings happen less often.
  • The zone feels smaller than Dhikala.
  • Permits can fill fast during peak season.

Dhikala Zone – Corbett's Most Iconic Wilderness

Dhikala remains the largest and most famous zone. People call it the heart of Corbett. Wide grasslands stretch for miles, and the Ramganga reservoir shines in the sun. Elephant herds walk slowly across open fields. Birds circle above the water. This zone delivers the classic safari picture that lives in most travellers' minds.

Key Features of Dhikala

  • Entry happens through Dhangadi Gate.
  • Canter safaris rule this zone.
  • The zone stays open only in season.
  • Grasslands and water bodies create rich biodiversity.
  • Wildlife density stays high throughout the year.

Dhikala suits wildlife lovers and serious photographers to capture the best moments of elephants. First-timers who want the full Corbett feeling often pick this zone. However, permits vanish quickly, so booking early matters. The zone closes during monsoon, which limits travel plans. Still, for many people, Dhikala defines Jim Corbett tourism at its finest.

Pros of Dhikala Zone

  • Huge grasslands boost animal sightings.
  • Elephants appear often near the reservoir.
  • The scenery feels grand and open.

Cons of Dhikala Zone

  • Permits run out fast.
  • The zone stays closed in monsoon.
  • Canter safaris feel less private.

Bijrani Zone – Where Tigers Roam

Bijrani sits close to Ramnagar, which makes it a favourite for short stays. Dense sal forests cover much of this zone, and tigers love these shaded paths. Grasslands break the trees here and there, giving animals room to move. Visitors choose Bijrani because it mixes easy access with strong wildlife viewing.

Key Features of Bijrani

  • Dense sal forests create perfect tiger cover.
  • Grasslands offer open viewing spots.
  • The zone sits near Ramnagar for quick access.

Pros of Bijrani Zone

  • Close to Ramnagar hotels.
  • Beautiful forest scenery.

Cons of Bijrani Zone

  • Crowds gather during peak months.
  • The zone closes in monsoon.
  • Permits are limited.

Jhirna Zone – Open All Year

Jhirna stays open through all seasons, which makes it a flexible choice. Travellers with sudden plans love this zone. Elephants wander here, and bears sometimes appear near the edges. Deer graze in open patches. The zone remains one of the most visited because weather rarely stops safaris.

Key Features of Jhirna

  • Permits are available more often.

Jhirna helps people who cannot plan months in advance. The zone offers steady wildlife viewing without strict season limits. However, tiger sightings happen less often than in Dhikala or Bijrani.

  • Frequent elephant sightings.

Cons of Jhirna Zone

  • Birding stays moderate.

Dhela Zone – The Hidden Gem

  • Rich birdlife and plant life.
  • Smaller crowds.

  • Excellent birding.
  • Peaceful atmosphere.

Cons of Dhela Zone

The Terai West Forest Division closes the Phato and Hathidangar zones from 30 June each year due to the monsoon. During this period, river and stream levels rise, safari routes deteriorate, and the forest department prioritizes wildlife protection and track repairs.

It brings together everything currently confirmed about The Koru Ville, a residential plotted township in Kilawali, Uttarakhand, developed by Sumiram Sai Realtors — its exact location, its legal standing, its plot sizes, its new villa collection, its amenities, and the practical, unglamorous steps of actually buying here. Wherever something is confirmed, it stated as fact. Wherever something is still in process — the project is now RERA-approved, for instance — that's stated plainly too, because a buyer deciding whether to visit deserves to understand the current status just as much as the completed details.

What The Koru Ville Actually Is

The Koru Ville is a RERA-approved resort-themed residential plotted township, spread across 3.5 acres in Kilawali village, Uttarakhand. It is not a resort, a hotel, or a holiday-home timeshare — it is a gated township where individuals buy land or a built villa and hold it as their own property, the same as any residential colony, except positioned at the edge of one of India's most visited forest landscapes rather than inside a city.

Two ownership routes exist side by side within the same gated boundary:

  • A standalone residential plot, where the buyer owns the land outright and designs and constructs their own home, on their own timeline, to their own specifications.
  • A turnkey villa, through one of three newly launched designs — Mayoora, Mriga, and Simha — for buyers who want a finished, move-in-ready structure rather than a self-managed construction project.

Both groups of owners share the same clubhouse, the same security perimeter, the same internal roads, and the same landscaped common areas. The township also includes a small restaurant-themed commercial cluster, intended to give residents a place to eat and gather without a drive back into Kashipur.

Where Exactly Is The Koru Ville? Location, Distances, and What "Gateway to Corbett" Actually Means

Near Jim Corbett is one of the most overused phrases in this entire category of real estate, and it means almost nothing on its own — Corbett's boundary touches multiple districts, multiple highways, and dozens of projects, some genuinely close to a safari gate and some an hour or more away by the time monsoon-season roads are accounted for. So here is the specific, checkable geography of The Koru Ville.

The site itself sits in Kilawali village, Udham Singh Nagar district, Uttarakhand, pin code 244712, directly along the Kashipur–Ramnagar highway — the main road connecting the plains town of Kashipur to the forest-edge town of Ramnagar. This corridor runs just outside the notified boundary of Jim Corbett National Park. The Koru Ville is not inside the park. It sits at its gateway, on the road that both tourists and residents use to reach the park's actual entry gates.

Distance to the forest itself: approximately 15 minutes by drive to Phato Gate, one of Jim Corbett's safari entry points. Phato Gate carries a genuinely useful practical advantage over several of Corbett's other zones — it typically stays open through the monsoon months, when Dhikala and some other core zones close for the season. For a second-home owner who wants year-round use rather than a strictly winter-and-summer property, that's a meaningfully different proposition than a project positioned near a seasonal-only gate.

Adjacent to the site: Tumaria Dam, within walking distance. It's a reservoir and wetland stretch known locally for birdlife and quiet walking trails — the kind of everyday amenity that never appears on a floor plan but genuinely shapes what a morning here looks like.

Practical, everyday connectivity:

  • Nearest school: approximately 15 minutes
  • AIIMS Hospital: approximately 34 minutes
  • Kashipur town (markets, healthcare, daily essentials): approximately 20 km
  • Gaushala Railway Station: approximately 11 km
  • Kashipur Junction: approximately 20 km
  • Ramnagar Railway Station: approximately 23 km
  • Pantnagar Airport: approximately 66 km

That last figure matters more than it looks. Why Kilawali's District Matters Legally — Not Just Geographically

This is the part most brochures skip entirely, and it's arguably the single most consequential fact for anyone from outside Uttarakhand considering a purchase here.

In February 2025, Uttarakhand's state cabinet approved a significant amendment to its land law (commonly referred to as the "Bhu Kanoon"), restricting non-residents of the state from purchasing agricultural and horticultural land across most of Uttarakhand's districts. The amendment applies to 11 of Uttarakhand's 13 districts. Two districts were explicitly excluded from that restriction: Haridwar and Udham Singh Nagar.

Kilawali — and therefore The Koru Ville — sits in Udham Singh Nagar district. That is a genuinely material distinction from projects in Nainital, Almora, Dehradun, Mussoorie, or most of the rest of the Kumaon and Garhwal hill belt, where the 2025 amendment now restricts non-resident buyers from purchasing agricultural land without additional government permission.

A few important caveats, stated as plainly as the advantage itself:

  • This exemption specifically concerns agricultural and horticultural land. The Koru Ville is sold as a residential plotted township, meaning its land has gone through the developer's own land-use conversion process rather than being sold as raw farmland — a different category to begin with, regardless of district.
  • Separately from the agricultural-land rule, current guidance for non-resident buyers of residential land across Uttarakhand generally references a cap (commonly cited as around 250 square meters, or roughly 300 square yards) alongside an affidavit process confirming no other qualifying holdings in the state. Whether and how this specific cap applies to a plotted residential township purchase in an exempted district is exactly the kind of detail that depends on current rules and the specific transaction structure.
  • Uttarakhand's land law has changed meaningfully within the last two years and continues to be actively discussed and amended. Any buyer — from Uttarakhand or outside it — should verify the current rule set and how it applies to their specific purchase with a property lawyer or directly through Sumiram Sai Realtors' advisory desk before treating any of the above as final. This section is offered as orientation, not legal advice.

Plots are allotted with documented registration. Pricing is intentionally not fixed in this guide — it varies by plot orientation, release phase, and current availability, and the only figure worth acting on is the one confirmed directly by Sumiram Sai Realtors at the time of enquiry.

The Villa Collection: Mayoora, Mriga, and Simha

For buyers who'd rather not manage a self-build, The Koru Ville has introduced three turnkey villa designs. All three are ground-plus-one (G+1) structures — two full floors — and all three share the same underlying idea: a private plunge pool and lawn at ground level, and a quieter, more contemplative space upstairs.

Mayoora — Built for Comfort and Calm

Mayoora is the most compact villa in the collection. On the ground floor: a refined living area, a spacious bedroom, a beautifully planned washroom, and a private plunge pool set against a green lawn. Upstairs: a second living space, a bedroom, a washroom, and a private balcony opening toward the surrounding greenery. Nothing about Mayoora is oversized — it's built around comfort and efficiency rather than scale, for owners who want the full Koru Ville experience without extra square footage to maintain.

The ground floor offers a more generous living area, a spacious bedroom, a refined washroom, a private plunge pool, and a green lawn, each given noticeably more room than in the Mayoora layout. The first floor adds a second living space, another bedroom, a washroom, and a private balcony — designed with slow mornings and long evenings in mind, which is, after all, the entire point of owning a home at the edge of a forest rather than in the middle of a city.

Simha — An Expansive Expression of Villa Living

Its ground floor brings together a welcoming living area, a private bedroom, a thoughtfully designed washroom, a plunge pool, and a green lawn, all scaled up from the other two designs. Upstairs, an expansive living space, a spacious bedroom, a washroom, and a statement balcony are designed specifically to frame the surrounding forest and hill views, rather than merely overlook them.

Choosing Between the Three

What Ownership Actually Involves: Plot vs. Villa, Honestly Compared

A standalone plot means owning undeveloped land and taking full responsibility for design and construction — the right choice for buyers with a clear architectural vision, a desire for full control, or simply no urgency to move in immediately. It also means managing a construction project from a distance if the buyer is based in Delhi-NCR, which is a genuine consideration worth planning for rather than glossing over.

A turnkey villa (Mayoora, Mriga, or Simha) means buying into a defined design with a shorter, more predictable path to occupancy. It suits buyers who want to skip the construction-management phase entirely and simply own a finished home.

Neither path is objectively superior — they serve different priorities, timelines, and levels of appetite for managing a build. Sumiram Sai Realtors' advisory desk typically discusses both in detail before a buyer commits to either.

  3. Document and eligibility verification. For buyers who are not Uttarakhand residents, this includes confirming current land-eligibility rules for the specific plot, alongside the standard KYC, PAN, and address-proof documentation required for any Indian property transaction.
  4. Booking and agreement. A booking amount is paid and a sale agreement is executed, laying out the payment schedule, possession terms, and specifications.
  5. Registration. The sale deed is registered at the relevant sub-registrar office, with applicable stamp duty and registration charges paid — figures that vary and should be confirmed at the time of registration, not estimated in advance.
  6. Possession and, for plot buyers, construction. Villa buyers take possession of a completed structure; plot buyers begin their own construction process, typically working with an architect or builder of their choosing.

Buyers unfamiliar with any step in this process are generally better served asking Sumiram Sai Realtors' advisory desk directly than assuming a generic national process applies identically in Uttarakhand — land registration procedures, required certificates, and local office practices vary by state.
